blocks.x: You say you've been working with Robichaud over there for... Harry Robichaud. Harry Robichaud. Is he the banjo player? Who? Harry Robichaud. Harry Robichaud, guitar player. Yeah, you know him? Yeah, I've heard him. I met him one time. Yeah. He's related to shots, wasn't he?
Yeah, I've been playing with him on that day, you know, for the last seven years.
That's Mardi Gras day, always.
Yeah. Remember the carnival clubs, these Mardi Gras, they have a dance every year. That's the two sisters?
Yeah. Like that.
You want to know, when you're born, how old are you? Well, I'm born. I'm born in New Orleans. Right here. What part of the town? I'm born in New Orleans.
I'm born in St. Philip, St. Philip. St. Philip and, let me see, which tree is that? Philip and Durbin. Durbin.
What part of the town? I'm born in 1898. Yeah. Born in 1898.
What is the exact date of your birthday?
Yeah, July the 15, 1898.
Can you tell us something about your father?
His name was Adolph Alexander too, wasn't it? Yeah.

My father used to play trumpet. He used to play trumpet. But after a while, he stopped playing trumpet. The way he was working, he broke his seat. He stopped playing trumpet, he started playing alto. Then he started playing baritone. He started playing baritone.
What band he was playing with? What band he was playing with?
He played on with Ben. He played with tuxedo band too for a while.
About how old was your father when he died? Do you remember when he died?
When he died he was 57 years old.
57 was old. When was that about? Exactly 57 years old when he died. And what year? Do you remember? Was that before the first war?
About 33 years now. About 33 years ago. I got a son 33 years old. I had a son about 3 months old at the time he died.
So that dates his life. Where did you learn to play? What was your first instrument? Who? What was your first instrument? What did you start on?

My dad had started me but he couldn't look like he had no patience to learn to teach me. He sent me to his friend Old Man Shalini. Oh yeah. And I took trumpet lessons. On the trumpet. I took trumpet lessons with Shalini.
Yeah.
And I gave that up and I started playing clannery. I went to Papa Teo.
How old were you when you started?
Old Man Teo.
How old were you? About how big a boy were you when you started? Who me? In music. Oh.
When I started on the trumpet I was about 15 years old. I was about 15 years old. When I started on the trumpet.
Then you took up the clarinet and went to Teo.
Yeah. After I gave that up. Was that Papa Teo?
Yeah.
That's right. Papa Teo. Papa Teo. I went to Papa Teo and I played and I stayed with him until he took sick. Until he took sick.
Well how long was that? That's about how long were you on the clarinet with Papa?
How old was I? Yeah.
About how long was I?
How long was I? Oh at that time? Oh about 19, 20 years old. Uh huh. How long you took lessons with him?
How long you took lessons?
Oh I went through a whole book with the old man. Oh yeah?
Yeah.
I went through a whole method. I method. Do you remember what book of you? Huh? Do you remember what book?
Which method?

I told Angy method. I told Angy. Yeah. I told Angy method right here. Yeah. I know that. I told Angy. I went through old Angy with the and the old man took sick right and I had about one or two pages left and I went with Piku. Oh really? Yeah. I went with Piku and took about two or three lessons with Piku finishing that book. The old man took sick. Yeah I was about 19 years old.
How was Piku? Was he a good teacher? Who? Piku. Was he a good teacher?
He was not as good a teacher as the Teal brothers. They were good teachers. You played the Alba clarinet huh? That's right. Alba system?
Alba system. Yeah. That's right.
Fifteen keys? Alba keys. That's right.
Alba keys.
That's right. Alba keys. That's right. Yeah. That's right. But I started playing Bohem system when I got in the Neary. Oh you did?
Yeah. And this was the second world war? No.
Second, yeah. Second world war.
Yeah. That's all it would buy for us. That's why we all had to play that. Yeah.

I started playing Bohem system. How did you like the Bohem system? Oh, I never forgot about the first music I had was when I had made up a band. Me and Paul Villar, half of them guys half dead. Was that a dance band or a brass band? A jazz band. A jazz band. Jazz band, yeah. Paul Villar, Edgar, Edgar Briscoe. Edgar Briscoe used to play guitar, huh? Who?
Edgar Briscoe.
Yeah, he used to play guitar banjo.

You remember him? Yeah, he told me that I didn't believe. Yeah, Edgar Briscoe. Yeah. He did the brickwork at my house. The house I built on down the night where he did the brickwork. But I used to play it.
Yeah, he used to play banjo. He used to play banjo.
Did you ever play anything else besides the clarinet and saxophone, Tads?
And the baritone.
You played the baritone?
I played the baritone, yeah.
How did you learn that, Tads?

Well, I learned that from learning the trumpet, which is the same thing, almost. And I, when I, during the WPA band days, I started playing baritone. They wanted a baritone player. And the professor in that band, he put me on a baritone. Told me to play the baritone. I could play the baritone. Well, I started playing baritone in the WPA band.
Did you have any lessons or pick it up by yourself then? I took lessons on the trumpet. On the trumpet, not on the baritone. You learned that yourself. The same fingering and all. Yes, yes.
I took lessons on the baritone. Which is the same fingering as the trumpet.
Was your father still alive then, Tads?

My father, he started me, but he started all my sisters and brothers. He started all of us, but he couldn't do anything with us. He had no patience. He figured, like, we should, we ought to learn quicker than it is.
Did your father ever play in any dance band, in any jazz band, or just a big marching brass band?

He used to play in the ragtime band. He didn't call them jazz band. But he played jazz in brass band. Brass band. He used to play baritone in a jazz band then. But before that, he used to play trumpet. He used to play in the ragtime band. Yeah, he played ragtime band.

Did he ever tell you when he started, or how he got his start in music, or anything when he was real young? Did he ever talk about, who? Did your father ever tell you anything about when he started in music?
No, he used to take lessons. He used to take lessons with old Frenchmen.
Old Frenchmen?
Yeah. He used to take lessons with the old French teacher around there during those days.
Yeah.
Yeah, my father, my father, my uncle, and my uncle.
So you had an uncle that played too?

Yeah. What was his name? Willie, uh, Willie Alexander. Willie? Yeah, but he didn't continue playing. He didn't, he didn't continue playing. He took, he, he was taking trumpet lessons with the old, old, old French professor around there.
Was he older than your father, or younger?
No, my father was the older.
He was the oldest. Yes.
Anybody else in your family played music, Tats? Who? Anybody else in your family plays music?
Yeah, I got a brother, my brother used to play music, play piano. Play piano? My brother younger than me, yeah. Yeah. That's good. Yeah, he used to play piano.
Did he get, did he?
Well, he's still interested in music, because he have organ, he, he, he, he, he have organ, he got piano, everything in the house. He works on a ship. Well, yeah.
Did he go to Professor Chalini too?
No, he went to a woman teacher, some woman teacher.
Is he older than you, Tats? No, he's younger than me.
He's younger than me. He's, he's, he's about, uh, about five, four years younger than me. How about your sisters?
They, they all start taking lessons. They all start, my daddy used to whip us.
Yeah. Used to whip us with a rule, try to make us learn. Yeah. He couldn't, he couldn't teach us. He couldn't teach us.
He couldn't teach us.
They all started, did your sisters start on the piano? Huh? Did your sisters start on the piano? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, the, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I,

I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I, I Paul Villar, Edgar Briscoe. I forgot some of the other guys.
Did you have a name for that band? Huh? Did you have any name for that band?
Yeah! After that, I started playing with Paul Villar. Not Paul Villar. With Omar Bernard. Omar Bernard, he is dead. The old trumpet player.
What was the name of the band? Huh? What was the name of the band? It was named after him. Omar Bernard. Omar Bernard's band.

It was named after him. Bernard after him. After him, I left him and joined the Tuxedo band. I joined the Tuxedo band with Ridgely and Celestin at that time. Tio is the one that recommended me to join the band. I played with them for about two, three years. I quit them until I quit to get married. Because they was going too regular for me.
What did you play in the Tuxedo band? I was playing Clannett.

I was playing Clannett, yeah. I was playing Clannett. And no, right before I left, they bought the saxophone. Oh, you got saxophone too. They bought the saxophone for me. Yeah. Yeah, they bought the saxophone for me. And I started playing my saxophone with them.
Was that tennis sax sax? Alto.

Alto sax, yeah. They bought my first sax. And after, and I left them, I left them, and I went playing with Man Perez. You heard of Man Perez? Yes, sir, yeah. Well, I played with Man Perez on the roof guard. Oh, yeah. I played in the roof guard. We played in the roof guard for a couple of years. Many years. Yeah. I played. I left the roof guard and joined Sidney. Sidney was playing on the hall. Sidney Desvene. Sidney was playing on the... On the... Capital? On the Capitol. That's right. Not the Capitol. Yeah. Capital. Sidney was playing on the Capitol. And he quit the Capitol. And he organized a band. He's owned. He's owned Ronnie. Well, I joined his band. He was getting work. And he had a good man. And I played with Sidney. I played with Sidney for a long time. Sidney's Sudden Syncopators. Sidney's Sudden Syncopators, that's right.
Was that mostly on saxophone or clarinet?

I played saxophone in Little Clarity II with Sidney. And I played with Sidney for about seven years, seven, eight years. After I left Sidney, after I left Sidney, I went to play with, how do they call it, that fella, that fella, you know, died. Celestan? No, not Celestan. It wasn't not Celestan. Not yet. That fella. He used to play violin. You talking about Pierron? No, not Pierron. I used to play, not that fella. Deathstone. No, that fella. That tall fella, you know.
Clarence Dersdun.

Clarence Dersdun, that's right. No, there's no way to do it. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And they're taking out. And Pierron used to get the work. Pierron used to get the work at that time. I used to play at the, at Freshina out there, Justin Parra. We played out there with Clarence Dersdun. And played there a while. And after that, uh, I came, uh, uh, things was getting bad. Things was bad then. Things was critical around here. Things was critical around here. And I always got on the Dub Pier. I got on the Dub Pier band. I got on the Dub Pier band, and I went to New York. When I went to New York, and I came back here, I came back here, and, uh, and Celestine called me up here. Celestine. Celestine called me up to join his band. I take the sick after Celestine.

I remember when you were at Celestine the last time. Yeah, I took a stroke. I remember, too, one time when you made those records with Bunk Johnson, remember, in George Lewis' back. Yeah, yeah, yeah, I played Bartholomew, yeah. Old Man Barbaran and all.
Yeah, I met y'all in New York at that time.
Yeah, a little after the next winter. Yeah, with Bunk Johnson. Yeah, the next winter you were in New York.
Bunk Johnson.
That's when you remember Gene Williams?
Yeah, I remember Gene Williams, yeah. I remember Gene Williams.
Uh, who?
He jumped out a window.

Yeah, he jumped out off of a building or something. Yeah, yeah, I heard about it. Do you remember who used to play with y'all with Manny Perez? Who? Do you remember the musician was playing with y'all with Manny Perez band? Who all was in the band with Manny Perez? Manny Perez? Manny Perez? Manny Perez? I played with Manny Perez. Oh, yeah.
I played Manny Perez in the Roof Garden.
Yeah, well, who's all in the band? The members of the band? Oh, who's playing with the band? Yeah.

Oh, they had Des Dune, not Des Dune. Maurice Durand. Eddie Cherie. Eddie Cherie was playing tenor. Tenor and Clannet. Yeah, I was playing Alton and Clannet. We had Kaffer who was playing banjo. And Mercy D, we used to play piano, but she quit. And the school professor. I see all the blanchets. I see all the blanchets, yeah. He played for a long time. And Willie Humphrey's brother was playing. Poison.
Was it Earl or what?

Not Poison. Oil Humphrey. Not Poison. The trombone player, Oil Humphrey. Yeah. Oil. Oil, that's right. Oil, yeah, trombone. He was playing trombone. He was playing trombone. And the bass player, I can't think of his name. He's dead. He's dead. I can't think of his name.
You from downtown here? You see, we stay uptown. Yeah, I mean, the bass player, where do you live?

You stay uptown. He was uptown. You know, you know the one that's got a son to let it carry him? Kimball, maybe. Kimball, yeah. That's right. Kimball played there for a while. That's right. Kimball. Kimball's daddy. He used to play bass there for a while. Yeah. But he quit. And they had another fella play. And I can't think of that fella. A fella died.
You spoke tank?
No tanker.
From uptown? No tanker. The bass player from another bass player? Why is the bass player? Yeah.

I can't think of his name. He had another game player. I can't think of his name. I can't think of his name. I can't think of that guy's name. But Kimball used to play. He used to play up there. And after Kimball quit, I just had a fella play.
What kind of banjo player you thought Caffrey was? Who? Caffrey. What kind of banjo player he was?
What did I think about Caffrey?
Yeah.
Oh, he was a good banjo player. Yeah, Caffrey's a good... Caffrey's a good... Caffrey's one of the best banjo players he had down there.
I never got to know him.
Huh? I never heard him or knew him.
No, he got killed. He got killed in Texas.
He got killed in Texas.
Oh, he had a gambling place or something in Texas. I think I heard about it.
Well, I don't know what he did after you left here. He's got some people live... Sister... One day... I'll contact one day. His sister... His sister lives around there.
His sister lives right there on there. That in Galveston.

Johnny St. Cyr gave me a picture of that... Johnny St. Cyr? I think he played there a little bit. Did he ever work with you? He what? Did Johnny ever play with you? What happened to him? Did he play or work in that same band? In the same band? With you? At the New Garden?

Oh, since the way he'd been away. Yeah, yeah. He used to play together all the time. And then... A long time ago? Oh, yeah. He used to write to me all the time, writing out from California. Yeah, my son used to stay... He used to run by his house. Mm-hmm.
Can you tell us any more about the bands that your father played in? What kind of... How big was the band that Golden Rule, when you were a boy? Did you ever follow those parades?
Well, the Golden Rule band is the only band that I know he played with. He played with. Besides, they had brass bands. You used to have brass bands rehearsal.
How were those brass bands when you were a boy? How big were the bands? Were they larger than the ones today?

Oh, the brass band was about... That one was 12 pieces. About 12 pieces. That's how big the band was. 12 pieces. Now, the Eureka start that... They didn't want to start that high in 10 pieces. Yeah, now it's always 10. Use 10 pieces. But there used to be 11 pieces.
11, 12 pieces. Yeah. 13, 10? 11 and 12 pieces. Yeah, yeah.

How many alto horns did they have, usually? How many on the alto? Was your father the only one? Or did he play with somebody else, like old man Barbaran? Or did they have two of them? Or one? One or two alto? How many what? The alto horn. Like your father. How many? No, yeah. They have one or two in the band?

No, he was the only alto horn when he first started. He was the only playing alto. Yeah. But he quit playing alto to start playing baritone. But the band used to use this one alto horn. One alto. Nowadays, they don't use the alto. The band don't use it anymore.
No, they use the sax. Did the old band have a sax in it?
No, they used sax.
No sax.
No. Well, Manuel Perez used to use saxophone when I was playing with Manuel Perez and Roofgaard. Yeah. I mean, on the street, though, in the grass bands.
Yeah, Manuel Perez used to use him and Eddie Sherry. Yeah.

Manuel used to use 12 pieces. He used to use 12 pieces. But he's big old. He used to play tenor with us sometime in the street. Nice play alto. And how they call him? Horse Manero? You know Manero Manero?
Yeah.
He used to play baritone.
Oh, yeah.
He used to play baritone at the time.
Horse. Yes, I'm horse.
Yeah.
Why did they call him horse, Tats? Horse? Yeah.

Why did they call him horse? Because he'd paw like a horse. I was always pawing. That's why he was calling horse. He didn't want you to call him horse no more. Of course, he might not get mad if you call him horse, but if we call him horse, he'd get mad. He'd get mad now. You want you to call him professor. He wanted to call him a brother. But he used to call him horse, but nowadays he didn't change his name. He'd been doing what I teach him now.
How many baritones did they use in the old days? The baritone, how many? One or two?
One baritone. This one, that's all he used. One baritone. This one baritone.

Did that play a part, something like the trombone, or was it always a different part? Who? What kind of a part did you play when you played your baritone? Was it something sometime like the trombone, or what kind of a part did you try to fill in? If you didn't say in a small...
You know, I'm kind of hard to understand you a little bit. I'm kind of hard to understand you.
I wonder what kind of a part you played on your baritone.
Oh, I used to play the treble clef.

The treble clef, too. I played treble clef. What you played? You played mostly like the trombone, or what instrument you played most likely? I used to play the treble clef. Yeah, the treble clef, that's a clip. It's a written part, of course. Yeah, it's a written part. I used to play the treble clef.

I was wondering, if you didn't have a part, like say in a church hymn, you know, some of the spirituals or something, if you had to just fake a part, you know, make up a part, what kind of a... Would you try to play sort of like a bass part, or would you fill in little runs, or what did you do?
No, I used to play mostly the baritone part. And it was those parts that they had there already.
Yeah.
And when I was in the WPA band, we used to take our orchestration and write a part, write a cellar part for the baritone. I used to write a cellar part for the baritone. Write that and play that.
Yeah.
Play that in the baritone. With the WPA band. When I was in the Navy, we didn't have all that in the Navy. We had all the music already printed.
Yeah.
Yeah.

Can you remember anything about the funerals when you were a boy? Did they march just like they do today? Have the same kind of funeral marches in the brass bands when you were a boy? Same kind? Yeah. When your father played, what kind of music did they use?

They played some of the same things, but I don't hear some of the funeral marches that they used to play. They'll be different ones. Yeah. But they still play some, but I don't play some of the funeral marches that they did here.
Were they difficult to play? Tense?
Who?
Were they hard to play? Fuel marches? Yeah.
No. Ain't no funeral at all that's hard to march. Marches easy.
No, I mean to play. To play.
Huh?
I mean to play the part.
You say they're hard.
Are they hard to play?
Hard to what? The funeral marches? Yeah. No. Ain't no funeral marches hard. It's easy. That's slow music.
Full time, you know?
Yeah. That's slow music. It's no, you just walk, walk and you're playing, you're playing slow parts. That's easy.
How about when you're coming back? Huh? How about when you're coming back?
It's harder.
It's harder.
It's harder. Jazz is harder than common times.
Why is that?
Huh?
Why? Why is it hard?
It's slow music. It's slow. Jazz is faster. You're playing jazz. You're executing. You're executing faster.
You're going to think what you're playing? Huh? You're going to think faster.
Well, yeah. Well, yeah. Yeah. You're going to think with these. It's already in your brains already.
But you just said faster execution. Huh? Faster execution, though.
Well, I was going to ask. I was putting down your name here on the box. What is your full name, Adolf? How do you spell that? My full number? No, no. Your name here. How do you spell your...
A-D-O-L-P-H-E.
It has an E on the end.
A-D-O-L-P-H-E. Do you have a middle name? That's my first name. Adolf, yeah.
Do you have a middle name, too?
Yeah, I got my middle name. L. Just L. Leonce. But L. Let's put L. Yeah.
I was going to ask you some more about the early brass band. What kind of a uniform did your father wear? What kind of... What color uniform? Did your uniform? What caps or what did they have?
Same kind of uniform. Well, same kind of... Well, on the contrary, they started using newer uniform than they did a long time ago.
Did they wear a coat in those days to have a coat on? Or now they use only the shirt sleeves?

They used to wear a coat. They used to wear this coat and dark trousers. They used to wear a coat. They used to wear a coat. They used to wear a coat. With that braid on. Yeah. With the braids. They used to wear a coat.
Did the golden rule have any special color? Blue or red or brown?

Yeah. Excelsior had a second uniform and the Man Peres band. The only two bands that had two uniforms was Man Peres and Excelsior. The Excelsior band was a band across the river and Man Peres was on this side. It was the band I belonged to. I belonged to Man Peres band. Yeah. Yeah.
Do you remember what the golden rule uniform looked like? Huh? Do you remember what the uniform looked like in the golden rule band? What they look like?
Yeah. Well, they used to wear a uniform like that. What color?
Oh, blue.
Blue? Mm-hmm. Blue with the braids. This is what you used to wear on the street. The stripe on the pants? Yeah. Yeah.
You used to wear that.
Yeah. You used to wear that a long time ago. You don't wear that no more. High color? The color fasten up here on the coat? They used to wear that.
The coat with the braids and the hook up here. Yeah. Yeah. Fasten up here. Yeah. Fasten up here. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

here on the coat? The sweater! The coat with the bread and the hook up here. Yeah, fasten up tight. Yeah, fasten up here. Around the neck. Do you see my own like that years ago? Long time ago. That changed.

Did they always have the music, the parts for your father's band when you were young? Do you remember those bands? Did they always have the music on cards or little books and put it on their horn, the lyre?
In the books? No. How did they do that? No. No. A foreign didn't get no, had no books. He didn't have no books.
They played from the music. Did they have the little sheet, little pieces of sheet music?

He had. He had a whole lot of music. But my mother told me to come in and take that music and separate it and keep the music that I wanted. And she went to burn it up. I didn't do it. She did away with it. Just like John Robichaud. John Robichaud had a whole lot of music like that. It was so all together. They were friends. Yeah, my dad had a whole lot of music.
Did he give lessons to other people or you say he didn't have any patience for you? What? Did your father have any other pupils? Did he give any lessons to other people?
Yeah, he had pupils. He had pupils. He had pupils. Looked like he had. But not for you. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hm.

One of my scholars is going to graduate at college. He's graduating music. How do you call his son? Oscar Ruzon. Ruzon. That's right. Ruzon's son. He's one of your scholars? Yeah. He's the first one I started in elementary. Did you teach mostly clarinet or sax? No, I started teaching clarinet. Yeah. And he's going to graduate in music. He's going to graduate in music sometime this June, I believe.
Did you have a lot of scholars, Taz? Who? Did you have a lot of pupils? No, I ain't got no more.

I ain't got no more scholars. I can't teach no more. My eyes is not good. No. My eyes is not good no more. I had a stroke. When I had a stroke, my eyes affected. So I can't. All I have to do is read the headline.
You still playing once in a while yourself? Who? Do you play anymore? Do you play anymore?

Yeah, I play. I play Little Jones. I play Little Jones. I play Little Jones. You play Carnicle Day, you say? The last Jones plays Carnicle Day. Well, I was going to ask, where did you get that name Taz? How did you? I called my dad at that. My dad was named Taton. Because he was short. He was short, like me. Call him Taton.
Well, where did you get the name? Well, where did you get the name Biscuit at?

Biscuit? Oh, well. Yeah, that's what we always called him Biscuit. I didn't know that. Biscuit, I used to work in a cracker factory. Making crackers. It felt like a cracker factory. And the people, and they started to call me Biscuits. I used to eat a lot of crackers. Biscuits. I used to call him Biscuits. I used to call him Biscuits. But my dad, he used to call my dad Taton. That's a French word. Yeah, he used to call my dad Taton because he was a short fella.
Did your father speak French part of the time?
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, my father was speaking. He was speaking Creole French.

In fact, he couldn't speak English too good because when I talked to him or something, he'd say some words but he had to say something. You remember him, Harold. Sure, I remember. You remember him then well, huh?
I never did 20 some odd years ago. I remember. I'm 52.
Huh? I'm 52 years old. Yeah. About 19 then when he died. I remember. I think he was that old.
I remember. Where'd your brother have? California.
Which part? Los Angeles. Los Angeles.
I used to call him the same house. I used to call him the same house.

I used to call him the same house. He was down there. Yeah? Yeah, he was here. He was still in the same house. He's been here all that time. He's been here a long time. Yeah. I got a son. He's a postman over there, you see. I used to teach him how to play saxophone over here. Tenor. And he was doing good. He was doing real good. He went to California and I'll give him John a sincere address. And he gave Johnny and Johnny, rent him a room. Oh, really? Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Johnny rent them a room. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Is he still playing, Tance? Huh? Is he still playing?
He plays around. He plays around a little around California. He plays a little around California.
You've lived in this house all your life, Tance? Who? You've lived here all your life? Not right here. No. You what? Used to live on Durden and St. Philip. Oh, I see. Yeah. Durden and St. Philip.
That's where you were born, you know. Who lived in Durden and St. Philip?
Durden and you. Oh, I'm born there in Durden and Philip. I didn't understand you. Yeah, I'm born in St. Philip and Durden.
When did you move here?
My grandmother used to teach school then.

segments.title: Mardi Gras work with Harry Robichaud
segments.summary: Talk of Harry Robichaud, and Alexander says he has played with him on Mardi Gras day for seven years, for carnival club dances.

segments.title: Birthplace and birth date
segments.summary: Born in New Orleans at St. Philip and Dumaine (Durbin), July 15, 1898.

segments.title: His father: trumpet to alto to baritone, and his death
segments.summary: His father played trumpet, then alto and baritone, with the Onward and Tuxedo bands, and died at 57 when Alexander's son was a few months old.

segments.title: First lessons: trumpet with Chaligny, clarinet with Papa Tio
segments.summary: His father could not teach him, so he took trumpet lessons from Chaligny at about 15, then switched to clarinet with Papa Tio.

segments.title: Finishing the method book, Piron, Albert-system clarinet and Boehm
segments.summary: He went through a whole method with Tio, finished with Piron when Tio fell ill at about 19, and recalls Albert-system keys and later switching to Boehm in the Navy.

segments.title: First jazz band with Paul Villar and Edgar Briscoe
segments.summary: He recalls the first band he organized with Paul Villar and guitar-banjo player Edgar Briscoe.

segments.title: Learning baritone in the WPA band
segments.summary: He explains he picked up baritone from trumpet fingering when the WPA band professor put him on it.

segments.title: His father's ragtime band playing and his uncle Willie
segments.summary: His father started all the children but lacked patience, played in ragtime and brass bands, and studied with old French teachers, as did uncle Willie Alexander.

segments.title: Brothers and sisters in music; father whipping them to learn
segments.summary: A younger brother played piano and went to a woman teacher; the siblings all took lessons under a father who whipped them with a ruler.

segments.title: Omar Bernard's band and joining the Tuxedo band
segments.summary: After his first band he played with trumpeter Omar Bernard, then joined the Tuxedo band with Ridgley and Celestin on Tio's recommendation, got his first alto sax, and left to marry.

segments.title: Manuel Perez at the Roof Garden and Sidney Desvigne's band
segments.summary: He left Tuxedo for Manuel Perez at the Roof Garden, then spent seven or eight years with Sidney Desvigne's Syncopators on sax.

segments.title: Clarence Desdunes, Dub Pier band, New York, Celestin and Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: He recounts later jobs with Desdunes, Piron, going to New York, rejoining Celestin until his stroke, and meeting the interviewers in New York with Bunk Johnson; Gene Williams is recalled.

segments.title: Personnel of Manuel Perez's Roof Garden band
segments.summary: He lists the band members: Maurice Durand, Eddie Cherie, a banjo player, Oil Humphrey on trombone, and bass player Kimball, struggling to recall others.

segments.title: Banjo player Caffrey and Johnny St. Cyr
segments.summary: He praises Caffrey as one of the best banjo players, who was killed in Texas, and talks of Johnny St. Cyr writing from California.

segments.title: Size and instrumentation of the old brass bands
segments.summary: He explains his father played in the Golden Rule band, and that brass bands had about 12 pieces with one alto horn.

segments.title: Saxophones in street bands, and Horse Manero's nickname
segments.summary: Perez's street band used saxes and 12 pieces; he explains why Manero was nicknamed Horse and that one baritone was used.

segments.title: Baritone parts: treble clef, WPA and Navy
segments.summary: He describes reading treble clef on baritone, writing his own parts in the WPA band, and having printed music in the Navy.

segments.title: Funeral marches and why jazz is harder to play
segments.summary: Old funeral marches differ from today's; he says slow dirges are easy to play while the return jazz is harder because of faster execution.

segments.title: Spelling of his full name
segments.summary: The interviewer checks the spelling of Adolphe and his middle name Leonce.

segments.title: Brass band uniforms
segments.summary: He describes braided coats and blue uniforms of the Golden Rule band and that Perez and Excelsior had two uniforms.

segments.title: His father's music and pupils
segments.summary: His father had much music that his mother burned, and had pupils though not his own children.

segments.title: Teaching clarinet and the stroke that ended it
segments.summary: His first elementary pupil, Ruzon's son, is graduating in music, but a stroke weakened his eyes so he cannot teach.

segments.title: Nicknames Tats and Biscuit; his father's Creole French
segments.summary: He explains Tats came from his short father, Biscuit from his cracker-factory work, and that his father spoke Creole French.

segments.title: A son and relatives in California
segments.summary: Talk of a son teaching tenor sax, and Johnny in California who rented a room to him.

segments.title: Where he was born and his grandparents
segments.summary: He was born at St. Philip and Dumaine, where his grandmother taught school; his grandfather played no music.

segments.title: Favorite band and Manuel Perez's band members
segments.summary: Asked about his best band, he talks of Perez's band, its players who did not read music, and trumpeter Oil Humphrey.

segments.title: Sidney Desvigne's band size and Poisey Seville
segments.summary: Desvigne's band had 10 to 12 pieces; Poisey Seville on banjo and Lewis Nelson on trombone are recalled.

segments.title: Maurice Durand
segments.summary: Durand co-led a band with Humphrey, then played second trumpet for Perez, and played parades with him.

segments.title: Small combinations and the Autocrat Club band with Paul Dominguez
segments.summary: He played many small jobs, including a band at the Autocrat Club with violinist Paul Dominguez, Ernest Milton, Ike Gravesen, Lawrence Stoker and Albert Glenny.

segments.title: Banjo player Johnny Simon
segments.summary: Interviewer and Alexander try to recall the banjo player in that band, settling on Johnny Simon.

segments.title: Violin players: Dominguez, Piron, Warnick and Lorenzo Tio
segments.summary: He played with Dominguez and Piron, with Louie Warnick on New York company jobs, and Tio in the Tuxedo band.

segments.title: Playing with violinists: Robichaux and others
segments.summary: He did not care for violin because violinists were bosses; he rates Dominguez and Bocage and calls Robichaux a businessman.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: The interviewers close the session and thank Alexander; the block is mostly garbled repetition.
